original_question: If p1, ..., pℓ are integer-valued generalized polynomials and T1, ..., Tℓ are commuting measure preserving transformations on a common system, must the averages (1/N) Σ T1^{p1(n)} f1 · ... · Tℓ^{pℓ(n)} fℓ always converge in L2?
target_in_paper: In the current arXiv version of 1103.3808, your draft matches Problem 14 in §5.2.1 (“Generalized polynomials”): the paper asks whether the mean/L^2 convergence theorem for commuting transformations with polynomial iterates extends to integer-valued generalized polynomial iterates. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.3808))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core mathematical content very well: it has the right class of iterates (integer-valued generalized polynomials), the right dynamical setting (several commuting measure-preserving transformations on one system), and the right conclusion (L^2/mean convergence of the multiple averages). ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
missing_details: The paper formulates the problem on a probability space (X, 𝓧, μ), not just an unspecified “common system.” ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

Each transformation T_i is assumed invertible, measure preserving, and commuting with the others; “measure preserving” alone is slightly incomplete relative to the paper’s setup. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

The quantifiers include arbitrary bounded measurable test functions f_1, …, f_ℓ in L∞(μ). Your draft mentions the averages but not the ambient class of functions. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

To be stand-alone, “generalized polynomial” should be defined exactly as in the nearby context: a real-valued function built from the identity function and real constants using addition, multiplication, and the integer-part operation; then one assumes the resulting p_i are integer-valued. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

The paper’s average is the sequence of functions A_N obtained by summing from n = 1 to N and asking for convergence as N → ∞; that asymptotic limit should be stated explicitly. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

For full self-containment, the operator notation should be unpacked as the function x ↦ f_1(T_1^{p_1(n)}x) ··· f_ℓ(T_ℓ^{p_ℓ(n)}x), whose averages are required to converge in L^2(μ). ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

The paper’s phrasing is “converge in the mean”; your draft uses “converge in L2,” which is faithful, but the paper’s exact formulation uses the mean-convergence terminology. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
refined_question: Let ℓ ∈ ℕ, let (X, 𝓧, μ) be a probability space, let T_1, …, T_ℓ : X → X be commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations, let f_1, …, f_ℓ ∈ L∞(μ), and let p_1, …, p_ℓ : ℕ → ℤ be integer-valued generalized polynomials, where a generalized polynomial means a real-valued function obtained from the identity function n ↦ n and real constants by finitely many applications of addition, multiplication, and the integer-part operation. Must the multiple ergodic averages A_N(x) := (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N f_1(T_1^{p_1(n)}x) ··· f_ℓ(T_ℓ^{p_ℓ(n)}x) always converge in L^2(μ) as N → ∞? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, in the terminology of §3.2, is the collection of sequences {p_1(n), …, p_ℓ(n)} always good for ℓ-convergence of commuting transformations? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
justification: This is the nearest paper-faithful sharpening because §5.2 first recalls the known mean-convergence theorem for integer polynomials under commuting transformations, and §5.2.1 immediately states that the challenge is to extend that result to generalized polynomials, posing exactly this question as Problem 14. The same nearby paragraph supplies the paper’s definition of generalized polynomial and records the boundary of known results at the time of writing (ℓ = 1 known; for larger cases the problem remains open even when all transformations are equal and weak mixing), while §3.2 provides the equivalent shorthand “good for ℓ-convergence of commuting transformations.” ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
